proposedTopics.title: Audit Process & Methodology
proposedTopics.description: How a smart-contract security review actually runs, end to end: scoping the codebase, building a mental model before hunting bugs, and balancing manual review against tooling. This is the operating discipline the rest of Phase 6 (classification, tooling, fuzzing, reporting) assumes. Resources: https://secure-contracts.com/

proposedTopics.title: Severity & Vulnerability Classification
proposedTopics.description: The frameworks that turn 'this looks bad' into a defensible severity: the OWASP Smart Contract Top 10 (2026) for risk categories, Immunefi's likelihood×impact scale for bounty/severity triage, and the EEA EthTrust levels for certification — plus what changed now that the SWC registry is deprecated. Resources: https://scs.owasp.org/sctop10/ https://immunefi.com/immunefi-vulnerability-severity-classification-system-v2-3/

proposedTopics.title: Static Analysis Tooling
proposedTopics.description: Automated pattern-matching over source code that runs in seconds and catches known bug shapes without executing anything: Slither (Python, the incumbent, 90+ detectors) and Aderyn (Rust, Cyfrin's newer analyzer, sub-second on large codebases) are the two tools every auditor runs before a human reads a line. Resources: https://github.com/crytic/slither https://github.com/Cyfrin/aderyn

proposedTopics.title: Fuzzing & Invariants for Security
proposedTopics.description: Where static analysis stops, dynamic testing over random/guided call sequences picks up: Foundry's built-in invariant testing, Echidna, and Medusa all hammer a contract with call sequences looking for a property that should always hold to break. The hard part isn't running the fuzzer — it's writing invariants specific enough to catch a real bug. Resources: https://book.getfoundry.sh/forge/invariant-testing https://github.com/crytic/echidna

proposedTopics.title: Security Report Writing
proposedTopics.description: Turning findings into a report a client, a bounty payout, or a public disclosure can act on: justifying the severity you assigned against a named framework, keeping the proof of concept as small as possible while still convincing, and writing recommendations specific enough to implement without another meeting. Resources: https://updraft.cyfrin.io/courses/security https://solodit.cyfrin.io/checklist

proposedTopics.title: Reading an unfamiliar codebase
proposedTopics.description: Auditing starts by orienting, not reading top-to-bottom: find every external/public entry point, trace which ones move value or change privileged state, and sketch a call graph of who calls whom before hunting for bugs. A codebase read in file order hides the actual attack surface, which is defined by reachability from an attacker-controlled call, not by file layout. Resources: 📖 https://secure-contracts.com/ 📖 https://updraft.cyfrin.io/courses/security
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: pick any contract in security/samples/, and in security/notes/<contract>-entrypoints.md list every external/public function, mark which ones move value or change access-control state, and draw a one-page call graph. Done when: the notes file names at least one function you would NOT have flagged as security-relevant on a top-to-bottom read.

proposedTopics.title: Audit scoping & the audit lifecycle
proposedTopics.description: A scope pins down exactly what's being reviewed before work starts: a commit hash (not a moving branch), a list of in-scope files/contracts, known issues excluded up front, and a fixed time window. The lifecycle then runs scoping → initial review → findings drafted → fix review (re-checking patches against the same commit range) → final report — skipping fix review is how 'fixed' bugs ship half-fixed. Resources: 📖 https://secure-contracts.com/ 📖 https://updraft.cyfrin.io/courses/security
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/notes/scope-template.md, write a scope document for a sample protocol in security/samples/ — commit hash, in-scope file list, out-of-scope/known-issues, and lifecycle stages with target dates. Done when: the template has a named commit-hash field and a distinct 'fix review' stage separate from the initial review.

proposedTopics.title: Note-taking and building a mental model
proposedTopics.description: Good audit notes aren't a transcript of the code — they're an evolving model of invariants ('X should never exceed Y') and open questions ('what happens if this reverts mid-loop?') tagged to specific lines, so a two-line hunch survives to become a real finding a week later. Auditors who don't write down assumptions re-derive (or forget) them every time they revisit a file. Resources: 📖 https://secure-contracts.com/ 📖 https://updraft.cyfrin.io/courses/security
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: while reviewing a sample contract in security/samples/, keep running notes in security/notes/<contract>-model.md: a list of invariants you believe hold plus a separate list of open questions/hunches with file:line references. Done when: you have at least 3 invariants and 2 open questions, each pointing at the exact line it depends on.

proposedTopics.title: Manual review vs. automated tooling
proposedTopics.description: Static analyzers and fuzzers are fast at pattern-matching known bug shapes (reentrancy-prone external calls, unchecked returns, arithmetic issues) but structurally can't judge whether the business logic itself is correct — 'is this the right formula for this protocol?' is a human question. A competent audit runs tools early to clear the cheap findings, then spends scarce human hours on the business-logic and cross-contract reasoning tools can't do. Resources: 📖 https://updraft.cyfrin.io/courses/security 📖 https://secure-contracts.com/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: on a sample contract in security/samples/, run one static analyzer (see the Static Analysis Tooling chapter) and separately do a 20-minute manual read; in security/notes/manual-vs-tool.md list what the tool caught, what your manual read caught that the tool didn't, and vice versa. Done when: you have at least one entry in each of the three columns (tool-only, manual-only, both).
prerequisiteTitles: Note-taking and building a mental model

proposedTopics.title: OWASP Smart Contract Top 10 (2026)
proposedTopics.description: OWASP's 2026 list ranks smart-contract risk by real 2025 losses, not historical folklore: SC01 Access Control, SC02 Business Logic, SC03 Price Oracle Manipulation, SC04 Flash-Loan-Facilitated Attacks, SC05 Lack of Input Validation, SC06 Unchecked External Calls, SC07 Arithmetic Errors, SC08 Reentrancy, SC09 Integer Overflow/Underflow, SC10 Proxy & Upgradeability. Reentrancy — the historical #1 — is now #8, because access-control and business-logic mistakes account for far more stolen value today. Resources: 📖 https://scs.owasp.org/sctop10/ 📖 https://owasp.org/www-project-smart-contract-top-10/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/notes/owasp-top10-2026.md, list all ten SC categories in rank order with a one-line reason each rank changed (or didn't) from your prior assumptions. Done when: you can recite the top 4 in order without looking and explain why reentrancy dropped out of the top spot.

proposedTopics.title: Immunefi severity classification
proposedTopics.description: Immunefi's classification system grades a bug primarily by impact — Critical (direct theft or permanent freezing of funds), High (theft of unclaimed yield or temporary freezing), Medium (griefing with no profit motive), Low (a promise unmet but no value lost) — then adjusts down for likelihood factors like requiring elevated privileges or unusual user interaction. It's the de facto standard bug-bounty severity scale, and auditors reuse its vocabulary even outside bounty programs. Resources: 📖 https://immunefi.com/immunefi-vulnerability-severity-classification-system-v2-3/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/notes/immunefi-severity.md, classify 4 hypothetical bugs (invent them, or pull from security/samples/) against Critical/High/Medium/Low using Immunefi's impact-first criteria, and note one case where likelihood (e.g. requires a compromised owner key) would downgrade it. Done when: each of your 4 has a one-line impact justification citing the Immunefi tier criterion it matches.

proposedTopics.title: EEA EthTrust levels & the SWC registry's retirement
proposedTopics.description: The EEA EthTrust Security Levels specification certifies a contract against three cumulative tiers — each higher level requires everything the lower ones do, moving from automated-analysis-checkable properties up to full manual review of business logic — and its checks were originally keyed to the SWC (Smart Contract Weakness Classification) registry. SWC is now deprecated and unmaintained; EthTrust and the OWASP SC Top 10 are the frameworks that replaced it as the working weakness taxonomy. Resources: 📖 https://entethalliance.org/specs/ethtrust-sl/v1/ 📖 https://scs.owasp.org/sctop10/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/notes/ethtrust-vs-swc.md, write 3–4 sentences explaining what each EthTrust level adds over the one below it, and why citing a bare 'SWC-107' in a 2026 finding is a red flag rather than good practice. Done when: you can name what changes between the lowest and highest EthTrust tier (automated-only vs manual-business-logic review) without re-reading the spec.

proposedTopics.title: Anatomy of a good finding
proposedTopics.description: A finding a client can act on has four parts in order: a title that names the bug precisely ('reentrancy in withdraw() via missing CEI ordering', not 'reentrancy issue'), an impact statement in the client's terms (what an attacker gains, who loses what), a minimal proof of concept that reproduces it, and a recommendation specific enough to implement without another meeting. Vague findings get deprioritized because the reader can't tell what's actually at stake. Resources: 📖 https://updraft.cyfrin.io/courses/security 📖 https://codehawks.cyfrin.io/first-flights
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: pick one bug you found (or seed one) in a security/samples/ contract and write it up in security/reports/finding-01.md with the four sections — title, impact, PoC, recommendation. Done when: a second read of just the title and impact (no PoC) tells you exactly what's wrong and how bad it is.
prerequisiteTitles: EEA EthTrust levels & the SWC registry's retirement

proposedTopics.title: Slither static analysis
proposedTopics.description: Slither is Trail of Bits' Python-based static analyzer: it compiles your contracts, builds an intermediate representation (SlithIR) over the AST, and runs 90+ built-in detectors (reentrancy, uninitialized state, incorrect ERC-20 interfaces, and more) plus printers for call graphs and inheritance. It's fast, has near-zero setup for a Foundry or Hardhat project, and is the tool every auditor runs first. Resources: 📖 https://github.com/crytic/slither 📖 https://updraft.cyfrin.io/courses/security
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: run `slither .` against a sample contract in security/samples/ and save the raw output to security/notes/slither-output.txt; then in security/notes/slither-triage.md classify each finding as real or false-positive with a one-line reason. Done when: you can name two findings Slither caught that you'd have missed on a quick manual read, and one you triaged as a false positive.

proposedTopics.title: Aderyn static analysis
proposedTopics.description: Aderyn is Cyfrin's Rust-based static analyzer: same idea as Slither (AST-level detectors, no execution), built for editor-integration speed — sub-second analysis even on large Foundry/Hardhat codebases — with a VS Code extension and a documented framework for writing custom detectors. Running both Slither and Aderyn on the same code surfaces different, only partially-overlapping detector sets, which is why serious audits run more than one static tool. Resources: 📖 https://github.com/Cyfrin/aderyn 📖 https://updraft.cyfrin.io/courses/security
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: run `aderyn .` on the same sample contract you ran Slither on, save the report, and in security/notes/slither-vs-aderyn.md list which findings appeared in both tools, which appeared in only one, and any clear false positive from either. Done when: you can name at least one finding each tool caught that the other missed.

proposedTopics.title: What static analysis catches vs misses
proposedTopics.description: Static tools reliably catch syntactic and structural bug shapes — reentrancy-prone call ordering, unchecked low-level call returns, uninitialized storage pointers, missing access-control modifiers matched against a known pattern — but they cannot evaluate a business rule against the protocol's actual intent, cannot reason precisely about cross-contract or cross-transaction state (that's what a fuzzer or invariant test is for), and routinely produce false positives needing a human to triage. Treat tool output as a prioritized list to investigate, not a verdict. Resources: 📖 https://secure-contracts.com/ 📖 https://updraft.cyfrin.io/courses/security
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/notes/tool-limits.md, write down (from your own Slither/Aderyn runs) one true positive, one false positive, and one bug class you know neither tool could have caught (e.g. a wrong reward formula) with a one-sentence reason why not. Done when: all three entries reference an actual finding or contract you looked at, not a hypothetical.

proposedTopics.title: Foundry invariant testing
proposedTopics.description: Foundry's invariant tests (functions prefixed `invariant_` in a contract that declares `targetContract`/`targetSelector`) run many random sequences of calls against your system through a 'handler' contract, re-checking the invariant after every call in the sequence — not just once like a fuzz test. A failing run gives you the exact call sequence that broke the property, often a shorter, more direct exploit path than staring at the code would find. Resources: 📖 https://book.getfoundry.sh/forge/invariant-testing 📖 https://updraft.cyfrin.io/courses/security
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in test/security/invariant/SampleInvariant.t.sol, write a Foundry invariant test with a handler contract for a sample contract in security/samples/, asserting one real property (e.g. sum of balances == totalSupply). Done when: `forge test --match-contract SampleInvariant` runs the configured number of sequences with zero invariant violations, and you can explain what the handler restricts the fuzzer to calling.

proposedTopics.title: Echidna property-based fuzzing
proposedTopics.description: Echidna is Trail of Bits' Haskell-built property-based fuzzer: you write invariants as Solidity functions returning a bool (by convention prefixed `echidna_`) or as Solidity assertions, point Echidna at the contract, and it generates call sequences trying to make the property false or hit a failing assert. It predates Foundry's invariant testing and is still widely used, especially where its corpus/coverage-guided exploration options go beyond what Foundry exposes. Resources: 📖 https://github.com/crytic/echidna 📖 https://updraft.cyfrin.io/courses/security
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: write an `echidna_` property function for the same sample contract you invariant-tested in Foundry, in security/samples/EchidnaSample.sol, and run `echidna security/samples/EchidnaSample.sol --contract EchidnaSample`. Done when: Echidna reports the property held (or, if it fails, you can read the shrunk failing call sequence it prints).

proposedTopics.title: Medusa parallel fuzzing
proposedTopics.description: Medusa is Trail of Bits' newer fuzzer — written in Go on top of go-ethereum for strong EVM equivalence — that runs many fuzzing workers in parallel across cores and steers exploration with branch-coverage guidance, inspired by Echidna's property/assertion model. Reach for it when you want Echidna-style property testing but need it to scale across a multi-core machine or CI runner. Resources: 📖 https://github.com/crytic/medusa 📖 https://blog.trailofbits.com/2025/02/14/unleashing-medusa-fast-and-scalable-smart-contract-fuzzing/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: configure medusa.json for the same sample contract, run `medusa fuzz`, and in security/notes/echidna-vs-medusa.md record wall-clock time and number of test cases run in a fixed window for both Echidna and Medusa on the same property. Done when: you can state, from your own numbers, which ran more call sequences in the same time budget on your machine.

proposedTopics.title: Writing good invariants
proposedTopics.description: A good invariant states something that must be true after ANY sequence of allowed calls, in terms an attacker can't route around — 'totalSupply equals the sum of balances', 'a user can never withdraw more than they deposited', 'share price is monotonically non-decreasing except on explicit loss events'. A weak invariant either restates something trivially true regardless of bugs, or is so narrow it only covers the one path you already checked by hand — the fuzzer can only find what your invariant is capable of catching. Resources: 📖 https://book.getfoundry.sh/forge/invariant-testing 📖 https://secure-contracts.com/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: for a sample contract in security/samples/, write 2 invariants in test/security/invariant/ — one about conservation of value (e.g. sum-of-parts equals total) and one about an access-control property (e.g. only role X ever changes Y) — and run both to a few thousand sequences. Done when: you can explain, for each, a bug that WOULD violate it and one that WOULD NOT (its blind spot).

proposedTopics.title: Stateful vs stateless fuzzing
proposedTopics.description: Stateless (plain) fuzzing calls one function with random arguments and checks a property on that single call — good for pure functions, parsers, and math (e.g. 'this square-root function never overshoots'). Stateful fuzzing (Foundry invariant tests, Echidna, Medusa in their default mode) executes a random SEQUENCE of calls across the contract's public surface and checks the property after each step, the only way to find bugs that require several transactions in a specific order — most real DeFi exploits are stateful. Resources: 📖 https://book.getfoundry.sh/forge/invariant-testing 📖 https://github.com/crytic/echidna
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: in security/notes/stateless-vs-stateful.md, take one bug class you can only trigger with 2+ ordered transactions (e.g. deposit, then a state-changing call, then withdraw) and explain why a stateless fuzz test on any single function couldn't have found it. Done when: you can name the exact 2nd/3rd call your stateless test would be missing.

proposedTopics.title: Severity justification in reports
proposedTopics.description: A severity rating without justification is an opinion; citing the exact Immunefi tier criterion (or OWASP category) you matched, plus the concrete preconditions (does it need a privileged role? a specific market condition? just a normal user call?), turns 'High' into something a reviewer can check and disagree with on the merits. The justification is also where you note anything that would downgrade a naive impact-only read — required privilege, unusual timing, or a mitigating control elsewhere in the code. Resources: 📖 https://immunefi.com/immunefi-vulnerability-severity-classification-system-v2-3/ 📖 https://updraft.cyfrin.io/courses/security
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: take one finding from security/reports/ (or write a new one) and add a 'Severity justification' section naming the exact tier criterion matched and any precondition that affects it. Done when: another reader, given only your justification section, would assign the same tier without seeing the rest of the report.

proposedTopics.title: Writing a minimal PoC
proposedTopics.description: A minimal proof of concept is the smallest Foundry test that reproduces the bug end to end — one setup, the exact call sequence that triggers it, and an assertion showing the bad outcome (funds moved, invariant broken) — with every unrelated setup step, mock, or helper stripped out. Padding a PoC with the whole protocol's deployment script obscures the one thing that matters: what a reviewer must change to make the assertion fail again. Resources: 📖 https://updraft.cyfrin.io/courses/security 📖 https://book.getfoundry.sh/forge/invariant-testing
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: for the finding you wrote up in security/reports/, add a Foundry test at test/security/poc/Finding01PoC.t.sol that reproduces it in the fewest lines you can manage, asserting the concrete bad outcome. Done when: `forge test --match-contract Finding01PoC` fails on the vulnerable contract and passes once you apply the fix, with no unrelated setup left in the test.

proposedTopics.title: Actionable recommendations
proposedTopics.description: A recommendation a developer can act on names the specific change (add a reentrancy guard on `withdraw`; move the external call after the state update; validate `amount > 0` before the transfer) rather than a general principle ('follow checks-effects-interactions') with no pointer to where it's violated. Where there's a real tradeoff (gas cost of a check vs. the risk it prevents), say so explicitly instead of pretending the fix is free. Resources: 📖 https://updraft.cyfrin.io/courses/security 📖 https://secure-contracts.com/
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: for the same finding, write the Recommendation section in security/reports/finding-01.md naming the exact function/line to change and the specific fix, plus one sentence on any tradeoff the fix introduces (gas, UX, a new edge case). Done when: a developer reading only the Recommendation could implement the fix without re-reading the Impact or PoC sections.

proposedTopics.title: The Solodit checklist as a working reference
proposedTopics.description: Solodit's checklist distills thousands of real audit findings (Code4rena, Sherlock, Cantina, private reports) into a searchable set of checks organized by category — the closest thing the industry has to 'here is everything auditors have already learned to look for'. Running it as a final pass after your own manual review catches known-pattern misses your mental model didn't happen to flag, and it's also where you go to find real historical write-ups of a bug class before you've seen your first live instance of it. Resources: 🔗 https://solodit.cyfrin.io/checklist
proposedTopics.aiContext: Build: after reviewing a sample contract in security/samples/, work through the relevant Solodit checklist categories in security/notes/solodit-pass.md, noting any check that surfaces something your manual read + tools missed. Done when: you can name at least one Solodit checklist item that applied to your sample and whether it was already caught or was a genuine miss.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why does an auditor start from entry points and value flow instead of reading a contract top to bottom?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Attack surface is defined by what an attacker can reach and influence — external/public functions and the state they touch — not by source order; starting there finds the reachable bugs fastest and builds the mental model (who can call what, who can move funds) that later line-by-line reading hangs onto. Pitfall: a function with no external caller in this codebase can still be reachable via a delegatecall, a proxy, or another contract you haven't looked at yet.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does pinning an audit's scope to a commit hash (not a branch) protect against, and what does the 'fix review' stage catch that the initial review can't?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A commit hash freezes exactly what was reviewed — a moving branch means new, unreviewed code could ship under the audit's name. Fix review re-checks that a proposed patch to a finding actually closes the hole and didn't introduce a new one, which the initial review (written before any fix existed) structurally cannot do. Pitfall: reviewing a fix in isolation, without re-running it against the rest of the in-scope code, misses fixes that break an invariant elsewhere.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: Note-taking and building a mental model
proposedPrompts.promptText: What should audit notes capture beyond a paraphrase of the code, and why?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Invariants ('balance never exceeds totalSupply'), trust assumptions ('caller is assumed to be the router'), and open questions, each tagged to a file:line — because a finding is usually a violated invariant you noticed days earlier, and without a note it gets lost when you move to the next file. Pitfall: notes without a line reference become unverifiable later — you'll re-read the whole file to confirm what you meant.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What kind of bug can a human auditor catch that no static analyzer or fuzzer can, and why?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A business-logic error where the code runs exactly as written but implements the wrong economic rule (e.g. a reward formula that pays out a token nobody put in) — there's no crash, no violated pattern, and no property to check against, because 'correct' behavior only exists in a human's understanding of the protocol's intent. Pitfall: don't skip tooling either — humans are slow and inconsistent at the mechanical pattern-matching tools do well.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Where does Reentrancy rank in the OWASP Smart Contract Top 10 (2026), and what pushed it there?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: SC08 — reentrancy is well-understood and largely defended against (checks-effects-interactions and reentrancy guards are now routine), while access control (SC01), business logic (SC02), and oracle/flash-loan attacks (SC03/SC04) account for the larger share of 2025's real losses. Pitfall: a lower rank doesn't mean 'ignore it' — it means the field has broadly learned the classic defense, not that a missed guard stops being exploitable.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does Immunefi's system decide severity, and what can override an impact-based rating?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Impact first: Critical = direct theft/permanent freeze of funds, High = yield theft/temporary freeze, Medium = griefing without profit motive, Low = no value lost. Likelihood factors — requiring elevated privileges (e.g. a compromised admin key) or unusual user interaction — can justify downgrading the tier even when the raw impact looks severe. Pitfall: 'temporary' vs 'permanent' freezing is the exact line between High and Critical — get the duration/recoverability right before assigning the tier.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: EEA EthTrust levels & the SWC registry's retirement
proposedPrompts.promptText: Why is SWC-1xx numbering considered stale in a 2026 audit report, and what should replace it?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: The SWC registry stopped being maintained and no longer tracks current vulnerability classes or terminology; OWASP's Smart Contract Top 10 (category-level) and the EEA EthTrust checklist (check-level, tied to certification tiers) are the maintained references auditors cite instead. Pitfall: some older audit templates and even tool output still print SWC IDs by default — don't treat that as evidence the registry is current.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What are the four parts of a well-formed audit finding, in order, and what does each have to do?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Title (names the exact bug, not a category), Impact (what's lost, in the protocol's terms, to justify severity), PoC (a minimal reproduction, not the whole exploit chain padded out), Recommendation (a specific, implementable fix). Pitfall: an impact statement that says 'this is bad' without naming who loses what and how much reads as unverified opinion, not a finding.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Enter one CodeHawks First Flight and write up your best finding using the title/impact/PoC/recommendation structure.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Register for an active beginner-friendly contest, scope-read the protocol using this chapter's process, and produce one finding write-up (even a Low) in the four-part structure — the real judge here is your report's clarity, not whether you find a Critical.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does Slither analyze to find bugs, and what's the tradeoff of that approach?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It parses and compiles the source into an AST/IR (SlithIR) and pattern-matches known-bad shapes across it — no execution, so it's fast and scales to large codebases, but it can only flag shapes it has a detector for, and doesn't know what the code is supposed to do (business logic), only how it's structured. Pitfall: a clean Slither run means 'no known pattern matched', not 'this contract is safe'.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Why run both Slither and Aderyn on the same codebase instead of just one?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: They implement different (only partially overlapping) sets of detectors written by different teams, so each catches classes the other's detector set doesn't cover; running one is cheap enough that skipping the second tool trades a few seconds of CI time for blind spots. Pitfall: overlapping findings from both tools aren't 'double-confirmed severity' — they're literally the same bug reported twice.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: What static analysis catches vs misses
proposedPrompts.promptText: Name a bug class static analyzers structurally cannot catch, and explain why.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A business-logic error where the code is syntactically fine and matches no bad pattern but implements the wrong rule (e.g. an incorrect reward-splitting formula) — the tool has no notion of 'what this protocol is supposed to do', only known-bad code shapes, so a semantically wrong-but-well-formed contract passes clean. Pitfall: multi-transaction/multi-contract state bugs (breaking only after a specific sequence of calls) are also usually out of reach for single-pass static analysis — that's what fuzzing/invariant testing is for.

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does a Foundry invariant test differ from an ordinary fuzz test, and what is the handler contract for?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A fuzz test calls one function with random inputs and checks a property once; an invariant test calls a random sequence of functions (via a handler contract exposing the allowed entry points) and re-checks the invariant after every call in the sequence, so it can catch bugs that only surface after several specific calls in order. Pitfall: a handler with unbounded/unrealistic inputs (e.g. an unrestricted mint) can 'break' an invariant in a way no real caller could ever trigger — bound the handler to realistic call patterns.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Sketch the shape of a Foundry invariant test asserting totalSupply equals the sum of tracked balances.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: contract Handler { Vault v; constructor(Vault _v) { v = _v; } function deposit(uint256 x) external { v.deposit(x); } } contract VaultInvariant is Test { Handler h; Vault v; function setUp() external { v = new Vault(); h = new Handler(v); targetContract(address(h)); } function invariant_solvency() external { assertEq(v.totalSupply(), v.trackedSum()); } }

proposedPrompts.promptText: How does Echidna decide a property has failed, and what does it do once it finds a failing sequence?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: An `echidna_`-prefixed function must return true on every call for the property to hold (or a Solidity `assert` must not fire); once Echidna finds inputs/a call sequence that violates either, it shrinks the sequence to the smallest reproduction it can and reports that. Pitfall: echidna_ functions must be pure reads of state, not part of any real user flow — mixing test-only properties into production contracts is a mistake auditors will flag too.

proposedPrompts.promptText: Write an Echidna property function checking total supply never exceeds a fixed cap.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: function echidna_supply_never_exceeds_cap() public view returns (bool) { return token.totalSupply() <= CAP; }

proposedPrompts.promptText: What does Medusa add over Echidna, mechanically, and what do they share?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: They share the same property/assertion-testing model (test-writing style is nearly identical), but Medusa parallelizes fuzzing workers across CPU cores and uses branch-coverage guidance to steer exploration toward unexplored code paths, aiming for higher throughput on multi-core hardware; being Go/go-ethereum-based also gives it a native API for embedding in other tools. Pitfall: more executions per second only helps if your invariants are good — a fast fuzzer restating a weak property just finds nothing, faster.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What separates a strong security invariant from a weak one?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Strong: a global property (conservation of value, an access-control boundary, a monotonicity guarantee) that any sequence of allowed calls must preserve, expressed independently of how you think the exploit would happen. Weak: something trivially true by construction (so it can never fail regardless of bugs) or scoped so narrowly it only re-checks the one code path you already manually verified. Pitfall: an invariant referencing implementation details (a specific internal variable name) breaks the moment you refactor, even with no behavior change.

proposedPrompts.promptText: When is a stateless fuzz test enough, and when do you need stateful (sequence) fuzzing instead?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Stateless suffices for properties of one call in isolation — a pure math function, an encoder/decoder round-trip, input validation on a single function. Stateful fuzzing is required whenever the bug depends on order or accumulated state across multiple calls (e.g. deposit → price move → withdraw draining more than deposited) — which describes most real-world DeFi exploits, since a single call rarely leaves a contract in an exploitable state by itself. Pitfall: a passing stateless fuzz suite tells you nothing about multi-call ordering bugs — don't treat it as invariant coverage.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What makes a severity rating defensible rather than just asserted?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Citing the specific criterion of a named framework (e.g. Immunefi 'permanent freezing of funds' = Critical) plus the concrete preconditions required to trigger it (privileged role needed? normal user call? specific market state?) — a bare 'Critical' with no framework reference or precondition analysis can't be checked or disputed on the merits. Pitfall: omitting a precondition that would downgrade severity (e.g. 'only exploitable if the owner key is already compromised') overstates the real risk.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What is a minimal PoC trying to isolate, and what's the test for whether you've minimized enough?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: It isolates the exact precondition + call sequence + observable bad outcome that proves the bug, stripped of anything not required to trigger it. The test: could you delete another line/mock/step and have it still fail on the vulnerable code and pass on the fix? If yes, it wasn't minimal yet. Pitfall: a PoC so minimal it no longer represents a realistic caller (e.g. skips an access check a real attacker would also have to pass) can overstate the bug's real-world reachability.

proposedPrompts.promptText: What separates an actionable recommendation from a generic one?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Actionable: names the exact function/line and the specific change (add a guard here, reorder these two statements, add this check before that transfer). Generic: restates a security principle ('follow CEI', 'use SafeMath') without pointing at where in the code it's violated, leaving the developer to re-derive the fix themselves. Pitfall: a recommendation that ignores a real tradeoff (e.g. a check that materially raises gas cost) reads as naive once the dev pushes back — name the tradeoff yourself.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: The Solodit checklist as a working reference
proposedPrompts.promptText: What is the Solodit checklist, and where does it fit relative to your own manual review and static analysis?
proposedPrompts.answerHint: A checklist of known audit findings/checks aggregated from real contests and reports, organized by category — it's a last-pass safety net for known patterns, not a replacement for reasoning about this specific protocol's business logic (which tools and checklists both structurally can't cover). Pitfall: running the checklist first and skipping your own mental-model read produces a report that only reflects what's already been seen before — genuinely novel bugs need the earlier chapters' process, not a checklist.

proposedPrompts.topicTitle: The Solodit checklist as a working reference
proposedPrompts.promptText: Work through the Solodit checklist against one contract you've reviewed this phase and log every match.
proposedPrompts.answerHint: Pick a category (e.g. access control, oracle usage) relevant to your sample contract, walk its checks one by one, and record hits/misses in security/notes/solodit-pass.md — treat any hit your manual pass missed as a gap in your mental model to close.
